name: Ferrogrip Pressline Assembly Night Crew Set
description: The workhorse uniform of the Ferrogrip pressline floor, worn by assembly workers on the second and third shifts when supervisors are thinner on the ground and the line runs hot. The coverall is a single-piece garment in deep charcoal synth-denim with Ferrogrip's red-and-black diamond logo heat-pressed onto the left breast and right shoulder. The fabric is treated with a light hydrocarbon-repellent finish that grays and cracks at the creases after six months of washing — a reliable way to date a worker's tenure. The torso features a full-length front zip with a magnetic storm flap, two chest pockets with snap closures, and aug-accommodation side seams along both arms: wide-gusset panels with hook-and-loop closures that open flat to clear a chrome forearm without removing the garment. Underneath, workers typically layer a Ferrogrip-branded cotton-analog tee in ash grey with the shift number printed on the back. Boots are broad-toed steel-cap lace-ups in matte black with oil-resistant outsoles and a reinforced heel counter. A wide canvas tool belt in tan sits at the hip, worn heavy with hex drivers, cable pullers, and a personal dosimeter clipped to the left side.
functionality: Hydrocarbon-repellent shell, aug-accommodation arm gussets for chrome forearm clearance, magnetic storm flap zipper, canvas tool belt with dosimeter clip, steel-toe and oil-resistant sole, layerable over thermal base
what_it_says: The cracking finish on the crease lines tells you exactly how long this person has been on the floor. Ferrogrip workers wear their tenure in the fabric — a brand-new coverall marks a probationer, a gray-creased one marks someone who has survived the pressline long enough to know which supervisors to avoid.
manufacturer: Ferrogrip Industries — company-issued uniform, boots from Ashgrove Linework
price_range: Φ160–Φ210 (company-issued; worker pays for replacements after first year)
story_hooks: A worker's dosimeter has been reading elevated for three shifts, but the floor supervisor keeps logging it as equipment error — the coverall's shift-number print on the back makes the worker identifiable in every security frame.
The aug-accommodation gusset on a worker's coverall has been sewn shut with red thread — a signal to those who know that the wearer is running unlicensed chrome under the sleeve.
A new hire receives a coverall that still has someone else's name patch half-removed from the breast — the previous occupant of that shift slot disappeared two weeks ago.

physical_description.visual_profile: Utilitarian single-piece coverall with a blocky, purposeful silhouette. The garment reads as industrial-grade armor for factory floor work—substantial, weathered, and marked by visible labor. On-body creates a unified dark canvas interrupted only by the Ferrogrip corporate branding and the practical geometry of reinforced seams and utility pockets. Worn with layered ash-grey undershirt visible at neckline and wrists. Heavy tool belt anchors the hip, creating a low center of mass. Overall impression: shift worker, veteran of the pressline, comfortable with machine noise and chemical exposure.
physical_description.fit: Relaxed through the torso with deliberate slack at the shoulders and upper arms to accommodate augmentation and layering. Tapered slightly at the waist via the tool belt's anchor points. Straight leg with room in the thigh for crouching and kneeling. The aug-accommodation gussets create visible width along the ribcage when closed—a design that announces 'chrome-ready.' Boots are wide-toed and planted, no ankle flex.
physical_description.primary_material: Deep charcoal synth-denim, hydrocarbon-treated. Undershirt is cotton-analog jersey. Boots are ballistic-grade leather composite with reinforced toe box. Tool belt is heavy canvas, tan/natural.
physical_description.texture: The synth-denim has a tight, industrial weave with a faint sheen from the hydrocarbon treatment. With age (and this set is meant to show it), the fabric grays and cracks at all flex points—elbows, knees, the inside of the collar—revealing the lighter thread beneath. This damage is visual proof of time served. The hook-and-loop aug-accommodation seams are tactile and load-bearing. Boots have a matte, oil-slicked patina. Canvas tool belt is stiff when new, supple when broken-in.
physical_description.color_scheme: Dominant deep charcoal with matte black boots. Ferrogrip corporate red-and-black diamond logo on left breast and right shoulder (heat-pressed, slightly faded with washing). Ash-grey cotton undershirt visible at collar and cuffs. Tan canvas tool belt. Small accent of dosimeter clip in industrial yellow/orange.
physical_description.closures: Full-length magnetic storm flap over the front zip (allows rapid one-handed opening under pressure). Snap closures on chest pockets (audible, reliable). Hook-and-loop (Velcro) closures on aug-accommodation gussets for quick access. Lace-up boots with reinforced eyelets.
distinctive_features: Aug-accommodation side gussets with wide hook-and-loop panels—mark of a pressure-line worker who runs chrome or plans to
Heat-pressed Ferrogrip diamond logo, deliberately placed to signal company ownership and shift assignment
Magnetic storm flap over main zip—a design detail that suggests wet conditions, chemical spray, or rapid suit-up scenarios
Visible wear patterns: graying creases, faded branding, oil stains around the tool belt attachment points
Embedded company-issued dosimeter clip on tool belt—radiation or contamination monitoring is normalized for this work
Shift number printed on undershirt back—marks the wearer as night crew (Shift 2 or 3)
Heavy-duty canvas tool belt worn low and loaded—professional weight that never comes off during a shift
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 3 (working class, corpo-employed). Company-issued uniform signals stable factory employment and baseline benefits, but the wear patterns and lack of customization mark this as floor-level labor, not management. The aug-accommodation seams suggest future aspirations or current augmentation financed through Ferrogrip credit—a debt relationship that ties the worker to the company.
physical_description.cultural_context: Wearing this uniform identifies you as Ferrogrip pressline labor, second or third shift. You are trusted with autonomous machinery and chemical processes. You are disposable by corpo standards, but your labor is valued enough to be clothed and equipped by the company. The visible wear is a badge of seniority—newer workers' uniforms are pristine and look cheap; yours look broken-in because they are. Augmentation is expected and accommodated. You smell like industrial solvents and machine oil. You know everyone on your crew by their callsign, not their government ID.
physical_description.condition_typical: Worn and weathered. The charcoal fabric shows gray creasing at all stress points. The logo is faded but still legible. Oil and chemical stains cluster around the tool belt and pocket areas. The boots are scuffed and the heel counter is worn down on one side from a habitual stance at the machine. Seams are intact but the hydrophobic coating is visibly failing—water beads unevenly. This is a uniform that has done its job for 8–12 months and will do it for another 12 if the worker doesn't get reassigned or injured.

Wide tool belt heavy with hex drivers and a yellow-orange dosimeter clip at the hip. Ash-grey undershirt visible at the neckline and wrists, shift number printed on back collar. Matte black steel-cap boots planted shoulder-width apart. The coverall shows visible wear—gray creasing at the elbows and shoulders, slight oil stains, hydrophobic coating failing in patches. Slight chromatic aberration and neon reflection on the coverall's creases. The model's posture is tired and planted—a stance of someone who has been standing for eight hours.
